cells.tense: What's coming toward your life is being met from a place that's already settled, and you're the one holding that ground.
cells.ask: Before you say the next real thing about something coming, put one line down on paper in your own words — good or not, it's yours before it's anyone's.
cells.core:
New things arrive into someone who's already at home in their own feeling. There's no scramble to prove you're alive to it — what shows up gets met from a steady place, and you let it come to you instead of going out to chase it. That's how the arrival stays whole.

So before the next sentence you say out loud about something on its way, write one line down first. It doesn't have to be good. It has to be yours before it becomes anyone else's, and what you keep is a small piece of the arrival that got named before it got spoken.

cells.tense: Something hasn't arrived yet and you're already standing in the doorway, rehearsing how you'll handle it.
cells.ask: Let one thing that's still in motion stay in motion for a day — no plan, no pre-answer — and notice what the waiting does.
cells.core:
Met well, what's on its way gets an open hand. You can feel it coming and still let it arrive on its own schedule, and the feeling stays in the room instead of running ahead into a conversation you haven't had. That's what lets new things land cleanly.

Instead you've already lived it — the talk, the outcome, the fallout — and the welcome is spent before the guest is at the door. Pick one thing still mid-course and leave it alone for a day. No plan, no pre-answer. What you're gathering is the feel of something arriving without your hand on it, and that's the ground the next thing grows in.

cells.tense: Something is at the door right now and the room behind it has gone quiet — the feeling that would reach toward it isn't reaching.
cells.ask: Get the two thoughts you keep circling out of your head and onto one page, side by side, no sorting — just both in front of you.
cells.core:
Met well, what's at the door gets answered. You can sit with what you feel and still move toward what's arriving, and the two don't cancel each other. That's what makes a doorway feel less like a riddle and more like a place you know.

The knock comes and the room goes still. Not cold — just not moving toward it. What's arriving is met with a held breath instead of a hand, and the stillness has started to feel like the shape of things. So get the two thoughts you keep circling onto one page where they can see each other. That gives the moving toward something to stand on, and the doorway stops feeling like a wall.

cells.tense: You're already feeling your way through what's arriving — the settling is happening — but you're talking about it like the situation is doing it to you.
cells.ask: Say one sentence out loud about something arriving: 'this is what I feel about it' — and leave the sentence alone.
cells.core:
Met well, the feeling you're having and the thing that's happening stay separate in your own account of them. What's coming gets met from a place that's already yours, and you know it, and you say so. That's what keeps an arrival from running you.

The feeling is already here — shaping how you meet what's coming, deciding what to let close and what to keep at arm's length. That's not the situation. That's you. So say one line out loud about one thing at your door, and then stop. No revision, no explaining. What you're hearing for is the gap between the feeling you carry and the thing that's only happening.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is in the Too Much cell if I write anything about what the person is braced for — the record gives the bracing, not its content, so the cell names the bracing and leaves the subject of it open. A reader could reasonably say 'sitting with what I feel is just how I think, not a capacity' — the cells narrow to what the capacity does in this seat rather than certifying that the person has it or doesn't. If the read is wrong, the asks still survive: each one is a small physical act (write one line, wait on something already in motion, put two things on paper) that teaches the person something about how they arrive at new things whether or not they recognise the card. The sentence that serves the writer most is any line that tells the person what their stillness is doing in their life — the record says the card is a condition of one capacity, not a portrait, and the cells should let the person test that rather than accept it.
